prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Banco Santander (Brasil) S.A." (ticker BSBR). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Santander Brasil does not fit the Rule Breaker profile: it is the number three private bank in a mature industry, with no top-dog position in an emerging market and no strong price momentum (the ADR fell from about $5.79 to $5.58 over the past year). Its only Gardner-style trait is a widely recognised brand backed by a global parent.
summaries.buffett: The bank is an understandable deposit-funded franchise that has been profitable every year since at least 2016, but its returns are mediocre (IFRS profit of R$12,766M in 2025 on R$125bn of equity, about 10%) and earnings swing with Brazilian credit cycles. Buffett would like the price (about 8x earnings and 0.8x book) more than the business, and the parent's pending exchange offer limits minority holders' upside.
summaries.munger: Munger would see a decent but not great business: scale and cheap deposits, offset by heavy leverage, rising credit losses (R$29.5bn of impairments in 2025) and strong competition from Itaú and digital banks. It is a fair business at a cheap price rather than a wonderful one.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms it is a slow-growing stalwart with a cyclical tilt: IFRS profit fell from R$15,528M in 2021 to R$12,766M in 2025, and consensus sees EPS down about 12% in 2026. At about 8x earnings with a 5% dividend yield it is cheap, but the P/E is not below its (negative) growth rate.
summaries.fisher: Fisher would note its digital investment and product breadth, but there is little evidence of superior sales ability or research that keeps producing new growth; return on equity has lagged Itaú for years. Management changed in July 2026, so the long-term direction under Gilson Finkelsztain is not yet known.
summaries.graham: On Graham's defensive tests it scores well on price: about 8.9x average 2023-2025 earnings and 0.83x book, so P/E times P/B is about 6.9. It is large and has been profitable for ten years, but it is a leveraged bank in an emerging market, and a 20-year dividend record could not be confirmed.
summaries.thiel: Santander Brasil fails most of Thiel's questions: it has no proprietary technology, no monopoly, and competes in a crowded market where digital banks have shown that the incumbents' products can be copied cheaply. Its distribution network is its main asset.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth compounders with operating leverage; Santander Brasil's revenue grew only 1.7% in 2025 and IFRS total income fell 0.7% in H1 2026, and it rides no major platform shift. It would not fit his approach, though the low valuation limits downside.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity and earnings momentum; here earnings are falling (2Q26 accounting profit down 25.8% year on year), analysts are cutting targets (HSBC and J.P. Morgan downgraded to Hold), and high Selic rates are pushing credit losses up. A possible catalyst is Selic cuts, but the setup does not suit him now.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high, consistent returns on capital without leverage; a bank with a 10-13% ROE and a 9:1 liabilities-to-equity ratio fails his first test. It is cheap, but 'good company' is the binding constraint.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula is not designed for banks, whose capital and enterprise value are distorted by deposits; on an earnings-yield basis it looks cheap (about 12% at 8.3x earnings), but its return on capital is modest.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a great business, talented and honest management, and the ability to reinvest at high rates; Santander Brasil has an average business, new management, and reinvestment returns around its 10-13% ROE. It does not fit well.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai might like the low price (about 0.8x book) and the floor set by the parent's exchange offer of 0.4056 SAN shares per ADS, but the setback (credit losses and an ROE decline) is cyclical and the upside is capped if the parent buys out minorities. It is a partial Dhandho fit at best.
summaries.wood: There is no fit with ARK's disruptive-innovation focus: Santander Brasil is an incumbent bank being disrupted by digital players such as Nubank rather than a leader in AI, blockchain or other innovation platforms.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and strong balance sheets; a leveraged, cyclical, number-three emerging-market bank does not meet those criteria. A control-holder exchange offer could interest an activist, but the parent already owns 89.7%.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale economies shared with customers; Santander Brasil keeps its scale benefits as margin rather than passing them on, and it is losing ground to lower-cost digital banks that do share savings. It does not fit his approach.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking huge new markets with technology; Santander Brasil is a mature incumbent, so his framework barely applies. The 'large market' leg is met (Brazilian credit), but there is no new product or technology wave behind it.
summaries.nash: On Tom Nash's 12-step process it fails most gates: revenue growth is under 10%, it carries more debt than cash as any bank does, its operating margin is about 22%, and it rides no secular trend. Its cheap valuation does not offset these misses under his rules.

momentum.evidence: The NYSE ADR closed at $5.58 on Oct 16, 2026, against about $5.79 in October 2025 and $6.11 at the end of 2025, so it is down over one year and year to date, while the US market rose.

g4.evidence: It is backed by Banco Santander S.A., which owns 89.7%, but CEO Gilson Finkelsztain only took over on July 1, 2026, and no well-known outside investors stand out.

g6.evidence: Analysts see it as cheap or fairly valued (consensus Hold, average target $6.77 versus $5.58), not overvalued.

simple.evidence: Taking deposits and lending is simple, but judging a R$1.29 trillion Brazilian balance sheet exposed to credit, rate and currency risk is hard for a generalist.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year from 2016 to 2025, but IFRS net income swung from R$15,559M (2021) to R$9,499M (2023) and back to R$12,965M (2025).

integrity.evidence: Disclosure is detailed (20-F, quarterly releases) and the board includes independent directors, but as an 89.7%-owned subsidiary its capital decisions serve the parent, as the July 2026 exchange offer for minorities shows.

b6.evidence: Recent moves have been simplifying rather than empire-building, such as merging the Esfera loyalty program into the bank in 2026, with no large acquisitions.

roic.evidence: Recurring ROAE was 12.5% in 2Q26 and 16.0% in 1Q26, earned on a balance sheet with R$1,161bn of liabilities against R$129bn of equity.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank, whose cash flows swing with deposits and loans.

b10.evidence: Equity attributable to the parent grew from R$119,492M (2024) to R$127,275M (June 2026), but profit in 2025 was still below 2021's R$15,528M despite years of retained earnings.

safety.evidence: At about 0.83x IFRS book value per ADS (about $6.71) and 8.3x 2025 earnings it is cheap, but with ROE near or below its cost of equity, book value may not be a conservative floor.

fairprice.evidence: About 8.3x FY2025 IFRS EPS (R$3.42 per unit) and a dividend yield near 5% is a modest price, even for a bank whose earnings are expected to fall about 12% in 2026.

mu5.evidence: The parent's support and an 11.2% CET1 ratio make failure unlikely, but credit cycles, Brazilian macro shocks and labour lawsuits are real ways to lose value.

reinvest.evidence: It can deploy capital into loan growth (expanded portfolio up 5.8% to R$714.8bn in the year to June 2026), but only at returns around its 10-16% ROE.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart or cyclical: a mature bank whose story is a recovery in ROE toward the roughly 20% management targets for 2028.

ly3.evidence: The P/E is about 8.3, but EPS fell in 2025 (R$1,629 vs R$1,708 per 1,000 common shares) and consensus sees a further decline of about 12% in 2026.

runway.evidence: Brazilian credit and investment markets can grow for years, but Santander Brasil's growth is tied to one country's economy and is in single digits.

ly7.evidence: Shares outstanding rose from 7,471M (2Q25) to 7,488M (2Q26), and no notable insider buying is reported.

ly8.evidence: It has little Wall Street coverage (3 analysts in S&P's US ratings, 6 for revenue) and only about 164 million ADSs held publicly, but it is a well-known bank.

fi2.evidence: It keeps adding digital and investment products, but none has shifted its growth trajectory.

fi3.evidence: Technology spending is not disclosed as R&D, and its results cannot be measured clearly.

fi4.evidence: It is strong in distribution (858 stores, 731 points of sale and 76.2 million customers), but not clearly better at selling than Itaú or Bradesco.

longterm.evidence: Management talks about a multi-year return to about 20% ROE by 2028, but quarterly profit pressure and dividend payouts dominate.

gr1.evidence: It had R$1.29 trillion of assets at June 30, 2026, and a market value of about R$106bn.

ni10.evidence: IFRS consolidated net income was positive every year from 2016 (R$7,465M) through 2025 (R$12,965M), according to its 20-F filings.

gr4.evidence: It pays regular dividends and interest on capital (yield about 5%), but a 20-year unbroken record could not be verified, and its units have only been listed since the 2009 IPO.

eps10.evidence: IFRS net income rose from R$7,465M in 2016 to R$12,965M in 2025 (+74%) while the unit count stayed about 3.73 billion, so EPS grew by well over a third.

gr6.evidence: The ADR at $5.58 is about 8.9x average 2023-2025 IFRS EPS of R$3.18 per unit (about $0.63).

gr7.evidence: About 8.3x earnings times 0.83x book gives about 6.9, far below 22.5.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology that is ten times better; its banking products resemble those of rivals.

timing.evidence: Falling Selic rates would help credit quality and growth, but in 2026 high rates are still lifting delinquencies (90-day NPL ratio 3.3% versus 2.6% a year earlier).

th3.evidence: It entered Brazil by buying established banks (including Banespa and Banco Real), not by dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: New CEO Gilson Finkelsztain ran exchange operator B3 for nine years, but he has no record at the bank yet, and it is not a founder-led team.

th5.evidence: It has strong distribution: 858 stores, 5,693 own ATMs, an app and payroll-loan channels reaching 76.2 million customers.

durable.evidence: Large Brazilian banks have lasted for decades, but digital banks and Pix are steadily eroding incumbents' fee and card franchises.

th7.evidence: There is no unique, overlooked opportunity; it competes in well-understood banking markets.

trend.evidence: It is not a leading beneficiary of AI or another platform shift, and digital banking is a trend that mostly helps its rivals.

dr1.evidence: 2Q26 accounting profit fell 25.8% year on year to R$2,667M, and analysts cut targets (J.P. Morgan to $6 in July, HSBC to $6.2 in September 2026).

dr2.evidence: If Selic cuts lower credit costs, profits could recover in 2027-2028 as management targets, but credit indicators were still worsening in 2Q26.

dr4.evidence: High Brazilian interest rates are raising delinquencies and provisions (12-month cost of risk 3.81% in 2Q26), which works against it for now.

dr6.evidence: The parent's exchange offer (0.4056 SAN shares per ADS, about $5.39 at SAN's $13.30 on Oct 16, 2026), Selic cuts and the new CEO's plan are identifiable events.

dr7.evidence: Falling earnings, a pending buyout of minorities and Brazil risk do not support a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is not a meaningful measure for a bank; net interest income was R$57,634M on R$162,495M of interest income in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank; its earnings yield is about 12% and dividend yield about 5%.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not meaningful for a bank because deposits and debt are operating items.

pa2.evidence: The fall in ROE from 16.4% (2Q25) to 12.5% (2Q26) reflects cyclical credit losses that could reverse, but competition from digital banks is structural.

pa4.evidence: At 0.83x book with a strong parent, the risk of permanent loss looks limited, but Brazilian currency and credit risk can do lasting damage in dollar terms.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: There is no fast-falling product cost curve opening new demand; its costs grew with administrative expenses of R$20,938M in 2025.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market is Brazilian banking, which will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its profits depend heavily on Brazilian interest rates, the currency and the credit cycle.

ns1.evidence: It does not pass scale savings to customers; low-fee digital banks such as Nubank compete on that basis instead.

ns4.evidence: Its position will probably remain that of a large incumbent, but it is not clearly stronger in 10-20 years given digital competition.

va2.evidence: Access to credit and payments is an important need, but many banks meet it.

tn1.evidence: It is an old-economy bank, not a company built for a secular trend such as AI or energy.

tn2.evidence: There is no gap between the story and reality; it is seen as, and is, a mature Brazilian bank.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap (about $20.9bn market value) operating bank, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline or startup.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable (R$12,766M in 2025), and revenue grew in 4 of the last 5 years, but like any bank it has more debt than cash, a miss that is structural to banking.

tn5.evidence: Debt (R$188.8bn of securities and capital instruments at June 2026) far exceeds cash (R$28.1bn), and free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank.

tn6.evidence: IFRS total income grew 1.7% in 2025 and fell 0.7% in H1 2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 1.7% plus a free-cash-flow margin that is not meaningful for a bank falls far short of 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 total income rose 1.7%, while administrative expenses rose 2.6% and credit impairments 3.7%.

tn9.evidence: It has more debt than cash and an operating margin of about 22%, and revenue growth is under 10%, which are instant kills under Nash's rules.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential legal threat, but labour lawsuits (a R$291M one-off provision in 2Q26), tax changes and the parent's exchange offer, which may lead to NYSE delisting, are material.

tn11.evidence: It provides bank accounts, loans and cards that help Brazilian people and companies manage and borrow money, and it charges interest spreads and fees; customers pick it for its branches, product range and the Santander brand.

tn13.evidence: About 30 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 5 (not checked), institutional ownership 5 (89.7% parent-owned), revenue vs expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 0, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue dipped in 2023, pre-tax margin fell from 38.7% (2021) to 22.3% (2025), and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: As a bank, total liabilities were about 9x equity (R$1,161bn vs R$129bn at June 2026), failing the under-4x test.

tn18.evidence: Gilson Finkelsztain became CEO on July 1, 2026, has no founder role and no reported open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: 1Q26 profit of R$3.79bn was described as below expectations, and 2Q26 profit fell 25.8% year on year, followed by analyst downgrades.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO or fraud suspicion, but margins have declined and there was a CEO change in 2026.

tn22.evidence: It has R$75bn of annual revenue, steady profits and no habit of selling shares to raise cash.

tn24.evidence: At about 8x earnings and 0.83x book, the price implies flat or declining earnings, below even its modest current growth.

tn25.evidence: Nash's free-cash-flow DCF cannot be applied meaningfully to a bank, whose free cash flow is not measurable in the usual way.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of about 7.1 is low, but with consensus EPS expected to fall about 12% in 2026, the PEG is not 1 or less.
